subject: biology

items.q: Which statement best describes variation between organisms?
items.correct: No two individuals are identical in all their traits, and the patterns of variation are the basis for classifying organisms.
items.misconception: Individuals produced by asexual reproduction share one genome and so are identical in all of their traits.
items.why: GCSE and MYP courses present asexual reproduction as producing 'genetically identical' offspring and identical twins as 'the same', and students slide from identical genomes to identical organisms. The word 'identical' in everyday use means the same in every respect. Variation between organisms is a defining feature of life: no two individuals are identical in all their traits. Even organisms that start with the same genome differ, because of mutations that arise during development, because the environment shapes many traits, and because gene expression differs from cell to cell and from individual to individual.
items.specStatementText: Variation is universal, and it is what classification is built on
items.random_wrong: Organisms are classified by a single distinguishing trait, so variation in the other traits is not used in naming them.

items.q: A gardener grows 50 plants from cuttings taken from one parent plant, so all 50 have the same genome. The plants differ from one another in height and in the number of flowers they produce. What does this show?
items.correct: Variation occurs between all individuals, because the environment and new mutations act on organisms even when they share a genome.
items.misconception: The plants must differ at many genes, since any difference in a trait requires some difference in base sequence.
items.why: At GCSE and MYP level a mutation is taught as 'a change in DNA that changes the protein', and most examples given (sickle cell) do exactly that. Students have not yet met non-coding DNA or the degeneracy of the genetic code. A single-nucleotide polymorphism is a position where individuals of a species differ in one base. Most of the genome is non-coding, and the genetic code is degenerate, so most SNPs are silent. A minority alter an amino acid or gene regulation and contribute to differences in traits and disease risk.
items.specStatementText: Variation is universal, and it is what classification is built on
items.random_wrong: The cuttings must have been taken from more than one parent plant, because the members of a clone are identical in every one of their traits.

items.q: How did Linnaeus define a species?
items.correct: As a group of organisms that share a set of traits
items.misconception: As a group that can breed to produce fertile offspring
items.why: Textbooks present the biological species concept as 'the definition' in bold, and students expect scientific terms to have exactly one definition. The name 'biological' suggests it is the one biologists use. The biological species concept is one of several competing definitions. It cannot be applied to asexual organisms, to fossils or to populations that never meet, so biologists also use morphological similarity, ecological role and DNA sequence differences to decide what is a species. Which concept is used depends on the organism and the question being asked.
items.specStatementText: A species as a group sharing a set of traits
items.random_wrong: As a group of organisms that can mate and have offspring

items.q: Which statement about the scientific name of the tiger, Panthera tigris, is correct?
items.correct: Panthera names the genus and tigris distinguishes the species within it.
items.misconception: The second word, tigris, is on its own enough to identify the species of tiger.
items.why: Students hear 'the species name' used for the second part and treat it like a personal name that stands alone. Common names are single words, so a single-word species name seems natural. In the binomial system the first part of the name identifies the genus and the second part distinguishes the species within that genus. Species words such as vulgaris, alba or domesticus are reused across many unrelated genera, so only the combination, for example Homo sapiens, names a species.
items.specStatementText: The two-part scientific name
items.random_wrong: It should be written Panthera Tigris, because both of its words are proper nouns.

items.q: The lion is Panthera leo and the tiger is Panthera tigris. What can be concluded from these names alone?
items.correct: Lions and tigers are two distinct species with similar traits that are classified together in the genus Panthera.
items.misconception: Lions and tigers look so different that they cannot be closely related enough to be placed in the same genus.
items.why: Identification in the field, in guidebooks and in the Linnaean morphological approach itself relies on appearance, so students treat visible difference as the definition of a species rather than as a practical clue to it. Linnaeus defined a species as a group of organisms with shared traits, and this morphological concept is still the practical basis of identification. But it has limits: male and female mallards look very different yet are one species, while some species of fruit fly are almost impossible to tell apart. How much difference counts as a separate species is a judgement, which is why other species concepts were developed.
items.specStatementText: The two-part scientific name
items.random_wrong: Lions and tigers are two varieties of a single species, Panthera, that interbreed freely in the wild.

items.q: According to the biological species concept, what is a species?
items.correct: A group of organisms that can breed together and produce fertile offspring
items.misconception: A group of organisms that live in the same area and interbreed with one another
items.why: Students remember that speciation follows geographical separation, and reverse the logic to conclude that separation alone makes separate species. The definition's word 'can' (potential to interbreed) is read as 'do'. The biological species concept asks whether organisms can breed and produce fertile offspring, not whether they happen to. A difficulty with the concept is that this potential cannot easily be tested for populations that are separated geographically, which is one reason competing definitions exist.
items.specStatementText: A species as a group that can breed and produce fertile offspring
items.random_wrong: A group of organisms that can mate and produce offspring of any kind

items.q: Two populations of a bird species live on islands 2000 km apart and have never been observed to meet in the wild. In captivity, birds from the two populations breed readily and produce fertile offspring. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.correct: By the biological species concept they are one species, though applying it to populations that never meet is a known difficulty.
items.misconception: They are two separate species, because populations that never interbreed with each other in nature are different species by definition.
items.why: Students remember that speciation follows geographical separation, and reverse the logic to conclude that separation alone makes separate species. The definition's word 'can' (potential to interbreed) is read as 'do'. The biological species concept asks whether organisms can breed and produce fertile offspring, not whether they happen to. A difficulty with the concept is that this potential cannot easily be tested for populations that are separated geographically, which is one reason competing definitions exist.
items.specStatementText: A species as a group that can breed and produce fertile offspring
items.random_wrong: They are certainly one species, because the biological species concept is the only definition of a species that biologists accept.

items.q: Two populations of a salamander have been separated by a river for about 10 000 years. They now differ slightly in colour, rarely interbreed where they meet, and the few hybrids are fertile. One biologist regards them as one species and another regards them as two. Why can both positions be defended?
items.correct: Speciation is gradual, so populations part-way through divergence are not clearly one species or two.
items.misconception: Speciation happens in a single act, so one of the biologists must simply have missed the event that created the new species.
items.why: Cladograms show speciation as a sharp branch point, and stories of evolution talk of 'the first' bird or human. Students also model mutation as a sudden change in one individual and extend that to the origin of species. Speciation is the splitting of one species into two or more, and it usually happens gradually rather than by a single act. Two populations that stop interbreeding accumulate differences in their traits over time; early on they are clearly one species and much later clearly two, with a long intermediate period in between.
items.specStatementText: Speciation is gradual, so some boundaries are arbitrary
items.random_wrong: Whether two populations are one species or two is a fixed fact, so a better test is all that is needed to settle it for good.

items.q: Which statement about speciation is correct?
items.correct: It is the splitting of one species into two or more, usually happening gradually as populations become more different.
items.misconception: It ends at a definite point that can be identified by testing whether the populations are separate.
items.why: Students expect scientific categories to be sharp, like elements in chemistry, and see species names in guidebooks as settled facts. The idea that a scientific classification can involve a judgement call is unfamiliar. Speciation is gradual, with populations becoming more and more different in their traits. For populations part-way through this divergence, it can be an arbitrary decision whether they are regarded as populations of one species or as different species, which is why taxonomists sometimes split or merge species.
items.specStatementText: Speciation is gradual, so some boundaries are arbitrary
items.random_wrong: It occurs at the moment when a single mutation produces the first individual of a new species.

items.q: Which statement about chromosome numbers is correct?
items.correct: Human diploid cells have 46 chromosomes, chimpanzee diploid cells have 48, and diploid numbers are even.
items.misconception: Humans must have more chromosomes than chimpanzees, because humans are the more complex and advanced organism.
items.why: Students learn that chromosomes carry the genes and assume that more genes, and so more chromosomes, must be needed for a more complex organism. Humans are habitually placed at the top of any biological scale. Chromosome number is simply the number of pieces into which a species' DNA is packaged; it says nothing about the amount of DNA, the number of genes or complexity. Humans have 46 chromosomes, chimpanzees 48, and the numbers across species range from two to well over a thousand.
items.specStatementText: Chromosome numbers vary between species and are always even in diploid cells
items.random_wrong: Human body cells contain 23 chromosomes in total, which is why a diploid number can be an odd number.

items.q: A student reads that a dog has 78 chromosomes in its body cells, a human 46 and a chimpanzee 48. Which conclusion is justified?
items.correct: Chromosome number varies between species, and it does not indicate how complex a species is.
items.misconception: Humans have 46 pairs of chromosomes and chimpanzees 48 pairs, one set from each parent.
items.why: The number 23 is heavily emphasized when gametes and pairs are taught, and students confuse the number of pairs with the number of chromosomes. The reason for the pairing, one set from each parent, is not connected to the parity of the number. A diploid cell contains two complete sets of chromosomes, one from each parent, so its chromosomes form homologous pairs and the total is an even number. Human body cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); a human gamete has 23.
items.specStatementText: Chromosome numbers vary between species and are always even in diploid cells
items.random_wrong: Dogs must be more complex organisms than humans, since they have the largest number of chromosomes.

items.q: Which set of features is used to classify the chromosomes when a karyogram is prepared?
items.correct: Length, position of the centromere, and banding pattern
items.misconception: Length only, so that chromosomes of equal size are matched into pairs
items.why: Karyograms are presented as chromosomes lined up in decreasing order of size, and students take the arrangement as the method. Banding and centromere position are rarely visible in simplified diagrams. Chromosomes are classified by three features together: length, centromere position (which divides the chromosome into arms of characteristic lengths) and banding pattern. Human chromosomes 13, 14 and 15, for example, are all acrocentric and similar in length, so they are told apart by their banding patterns; chromosomes of similar length elsewhere in the karyogram are separated by centromere position as well.
items.specStatementText: Karyograms, and the testable idea that chromosome 2 is a fusion
items.random_wrong: Number of genes and total amount of DNA in each chromosome

items.q: Human chromosome 2 contains telomere-like sequences near its middle and a second, inactive centromere region, and its banding pattern matches the two chimpanzee chromosomes formerly numbered 12 and 13 placed end to end. How well does this evidence support the hypothesis that chromosome 2 arose by fusion of two chromosomes in a shared primate ancestor?
items.correct: Strongly: the fusion hypothesis predicts exactly these features, and none would be expected if a chromosome pair had simply been lost.
items.misconception: Weakly: the simpler explanation is that humans lost one whole chromosome pair, which requires no fused chromosome.
items.why: '46 versus 48' invites subtraction, and 'losing a chromosome' is the simplest story. Students have met chromosome loss in the context of non-disjunction and assume loss is the usual way numbers change. Losing a whole chromosome pair would remove hundreds of genes and be lethal. The fusion hypothesis is supported by evidence: human chromosome 2 has telomere-like sequences in its middle, a second inactive centromere region, and banding that matches chimpanzee chromosomes 2A and 2B (formerly numbered 12 and 13) placed end to end.
items.specStatementText: Karyograms, and the testable idea that chromosome 2 is a fusion
items.random_wrong: Not at all: the fusion happened millions of years ago, so no observation made today can test what actually occurred.

items.q: A student claims: 'The fusion that formed human chromosome 2 happened too long ago to be tested scientifically.' Which response is correct?
items.correct: The hypothesis is testable, because it predicts observable features of chromosome 2 that might have been absent.
items.misconception: The student is right: a hypothesis about a past event cannot be tested because the event itself cannot be repeated.
items.why: Science lessons equate 'testing' with doing a controlled experiment, and students have not separated the two ideas of repeating an event and checking a prediction that follows from it. A testable hypothesis is one whose predictions can be checked by observation or experiment and could turn out to be wrong. The origin of chromosome 2 by fusion is testable: if it were false, chromosome 2 would not carry internal telomere sequences and a vestigial centromere. A non-testable statement, such as a claim about which species is 'most beautiful', makes no prediction that any observation could contradict.
items.specStatementText: Karyograms, and the testable idea that chromosome 2 is a fusion
items.random_wrong: The hypothesis is testable only because most scientists have now accepted that the fusion took place.

items.q: What is meant by the genome of an organism?
items.correct: All of the genetic information of the organism, including non-coding DNA
items.misconception: The set of genes that is identical in every member of the organism's species
items.why: 'The human genome' is spoken of as one thing, and the Human Genome Project 'sequenced the human genome', so students picture a single shared blueprint. Genes and alleles are taught as the level at which individuals differ, and the genome is assumed to sit above that. The genome is all the genetic information of an organism, and it is unique to that individual (other than in clones). Organisms in the same species share most of their genome, but variations such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms, of which any two humans differ at millions of positions, give diversity within the species.
items.specStatementText: Within a species, genomes are mostly shared but never identical
items.random_wrong: The number of chromosomes in each of the organism's diploid body cells

items.q: Two unrelated people have their genomes sequenced. At one position on chromosome 7, in a region between genes, one person has T and the other has C. What is the best description of this difference?
items.correct: A single-nucleotide polymorphism that is unlikely to affect either person's traits
items.misconception: A variant that fixes which diseases each of the two people will develop later in life
items.why: Single-gene conditions such as cystic fibrosis are the examples students learn, and in those the genotype does predict the disease. Media language about 'the gene for' a condition extends this determinism to all traits. Personalized medicine, a potential future use of whole genome sequencing, means using an individual's genome to estimate disease risks, to choose drugs and doses that suit their genotype, and to match treatments to the mutations in a tumour. For most diseases many genes and the environment interact, so the sequence changes probabilities rather than fixing outcomes.
items.specStatementText: Within a species, genomes are mostly shared but never identical
items.random_wrong: A mutation that must alter a protein, so the two people will differ in some visible trait

items.q: From a genome size database a student extracts these values: fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) about 180 million base pairs; human about 3100 million; bread wheat about 17 000 million; the flowering plant Paris japonica about 150 000 million. What do the data show about genome size and organism complexity?
items.correct: Genome size varies enormously and does not increase with complexity, since two plants have genomes far larger than the human genome.
items.misconception: Paris japonica must be the most complex organism of the four, because it has by far the largest genome of them.
items.why: Genome is equated with 'the instructions for building the organism', and more elaborate organisms are assumed to need longer instructions. Students also assume genome size is proportional to gene number. Genome size is the total amount of DNA, most of which in eukaryotes is non-coding. Data from genome size databases show that some amphibians and flowering plants have genomes tens of times larger than the human 3.1 gigabase genome, while some more complex animals have smaller genomes than simpler ones. Complexity is not predicted by genome size.
items.specStatementText: Comparing genome sizes across groups
items.random_wrong: Wheat and Paris japonica must have many more chromosomes than humans, since genome size depends on chromosome number.

items.q: Which statement about whole genome sequencing is correct?
items.correct: Its cost has fallen and its speed has increased, and it is used in research into evolutionary relationships.
items.misconception: Sequencing a single complete human genome still takes several years and costs many hundreds of millions of dollars.
items.why: The Human Genome Project (1990 to 2003, around three billion dollars) is the headline example most students have met, and its figures are remembered as if they were current. Whole genome sequencing has become steadily faster and cheaper, from over a decade and billions of dollars for the first human genome to about a day and hundreds of dollars now. This is why it can be used routinely in research into evolutionary relationships and why personalized medicine is a realistic future use.
items.specStatementText: What genome sequencing is used for now, and might be soon
items.random_wrong: It is used routinely to tell each patient exactly which diseases they will develop and when.

items.q: A hospital proposes to sequence the whole genome of every patient diagnosed with cancer. Which is the most accurate description of what this could achieve?
items.correct: Treatment could be matched to the particular mutations in each patient's tumour, a form of personalized medicine.
items.misconception: Each patient's exact future diseases could be read straight from the sequence, so no further diagnosis would be needed.
items.why: Single-gene conditions such as cystic fibrosis are the examples students learn, and in those the genotype does predict the disease. Media language about 'the gene for' a condition extends this determinism to all traits. Personalized medicine, a potential future use of whole genome sequencing, means using an individual's genome to estimate disease risks, to choose drugs and doses that suit their genotype, and to match treatments to the mutations in a tumour. For most diseases many genes and the environment interact, so the sequence changes probabilities rather than fixing outcomes.
items.specStatementText: What genome sequencing is used for now, and might be soon
items.random_wrong: The plan is unrealistic, because each genome would take several years to sequence and cost many millions of dollars.

items.q: Genes for antibiotic resistance carried on a plasmid in Escherichia coli have been found with an identical base sequence in Klebsiella pneumoniae, a bacterium of a different genus. Why does this create difficulty for the biological species concept?
items.correct: Genes are being transferred between species, so bacterial gene pools are not closed.
items.misconception: It shows the two bacteria have been breeding together, so they must be members of a single species.
items.why: Conjugation is sometimes described loosely as 'bacterial sex', and students map it onto sexual reproduction. They assume gene exchange is limited to a species, as it is in sexually reproducing eukaryotes. The biological species concept does not work well where genes can be transferred from one species to another. Horizontal gene transfer between bacteria of different species, for example of antibiotic resistance genes on plasmids, means bacterial 'species' do not have the closed gene pools the concept requires, and bacterial species are defined by other criteria such as DNA sequence similarity.
items.specStatementText: Why the biological species concept fails for asexual organisms and bacteria
items.random_wrong: Bacteria do not reproduce sexually, and so they cannot be placed in any species at all.

items.q: A horse has 64 chromosomes in its body cells and a donkey has 62. They can mate to produce a mule. Which statement correctly explains why mules are almost always sterile?
items.correct: The mule's 63 chromosomes cannot all form homologous pairs in meiosis, so viable gametes are rarely produced.
items.misconception: The mule's body cells cannot complete mitosis, because an odd number of chromosomes cannot be split equally.
items.why: Students learn that meiosis requires pairing and that mitosis and meiosis are both 'cell division', so they conflate the two. They also expect a chromosome mismatch to stop development, not just reproduction. Mitosis copies and separates chromosomes individually, so a mule with 63 chromosomes grows normally. Meiosis requires homologous chromosomes to pair, and with unequal parental sets many chromosomes have no partner, so viable gametes are almost never formed. Cross-breeding between species with different chromosome numbers is therefore unlikely to give fertile offspring.
items.specStatementText: Chromosome number is shared within a species
items.random_wrong: Horses and donkeys are one species because they produce offspring, so the mule is not a hybrid at all.

items.q: A student is constructing a dichotomous key to identify five species of tree growing in a local park. Which first step is the best design?
items.correct: 1a Leaves arranged in opposite pairs, go to 2; 1b Leaves arranged alternately, go to 4
items.misconception: 1a Tree more than 10 m tall, go to 2; 1b Tree less than 10 m tall, go to 4
items.why: Size and colour are the features students notice first when they look at local organisms, and a key is drafted from the particular specimens in front of them without asking whether other individuals would share the feature. A dichotomous key must work for any individual of the species, so each step should use a trait that is present in all members and easily observed. Continuous or variable traits such as 'large' or 'bright green' lead different users to different answers.
items.specStatementText: Building a dichotomous key for local species
items.random_wrong: 1a Leaves needle-like, species A; 1b Leaves broad, species B; 1c Leaves scaly, species C

items.q: Water samples from a pond were filtered, the DNA in them was extracted, and a barcode region was sequenced. Sequences matching the reference barcode of the great crested newt were found, although no newts were seen during the survey. Which is the best interpretation?
items.correct: Newts probably use the pond, because eDNA barcoding is a sensitive method, though the DNA could have been carried in.
items.misconception: A living newt was certainly present at the exact spot and time of sampling, since eDNA occurs only where the organism is.
items.why: Students equate DNA with the organism and do not think of DNA as material that is shed, persists and moves independently of its source. eDNA is DNA shed into the environment in cells, mucus, faeces and other material. It allows rapid, sensitive surveys of biodiversity, but results need care in interpretation: DNA can be transported downstream, can persist after an organism leaves or dies, and can come from a predator's faeces or from contamination.
items.specStatementText: Reading a habitat's species from environmental DNA
items.random_wrong: The result is unreliable, because only a short region of DNA was sequenced, rather than the complete genome of the newt species.

items.q: Five chromosomes from one metaphase spread are described. V: long, centromere near the middle, dark bands near both ends. W: long, centromere near the middle, dark bands near both ends. X: long, centromere near the middle, one dark band near one end only. Y: long, centromere near one end, dark bands near both ends. Z: short, centromere near the middle, dark bands near both ends. Which two chromosomes should be placed together as a homologous pair in the karyogram?
items.correct: V and W, because they match one another in length, centromere position and banding pattern
items.misconception: W and Y, because their length and banding match and centromere position is not used to match homologues
items.why: GCSE and MYP diagrams draw every chromosome as a symmetrical X with the centromere at the centre, and students have rarely looked at a real metaphase spread in which many chromosomes are clearly lopsided. Centromere position varies between chromosomes and is constant for a given chromosome, which is why it is one of the three features, with length and banding pattern, used to classify chromosomes in a karyogram. Human chromosomes 13, 14 and 15, for instance, have the centromere very near one end, whereas chromosome 1 has it near the middle.
items.specStatementText: Karyograms, and the testable idea that chromosome 2 is a fusion
items.random_wrong: W and X, because homologous chromosomes are simply the two chromosomes that share the same length

items.q: On what basis are organisms named and classified?
items.correct: On the complex patterns of variation across many traits, so that organisms sharing a whole set of traits are grouped together; a single obvious trait is not enough.
items.misconception: An organism is classified by one obvious feature: anything that swims is a fish, anything that flies is a bird, and anything green that grows in the ground is a plant.
items.why: Young children learn to sort living things by one salient feature, and everyday names such as 'jellyfish', 'starfish' and 'seaweed' embed a single-trait classification. Students carry this into biology without noticing that whales, bats and fungi break it. The patterns of variation between organisms are complex, and it is these whole patterns, not one trait, that are the basis for naming and classifying organisms. A whale shares with mammals a suite of traits (hair, milk, lungs, three ear bones, a four-chambered heart) that outweigh the one trait it shares with fish.
items.specStatementText: Variation is universal, and it is what classification is built on
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How should a binomial name be written?
items.correct: With the genus name given an initial capital letter and the species name entirely lowercase, for example Homo sapiens (in italics when printed).
items.misconception: Both parts of the scientific name are proper nouns and should each begin with a capital letter, as in 'Homo Sapiens'.
items.why: Students know the names are Latin and formal, and English capitalizes proper names, so capitalizing both words feels correct. Some also copy the capitalized style of common names such as 'Bald Eagle'. The convention is fixed: the genus name is given an initial capital letter and the species name is lowercase, even when it is derived from a person's name or place. Homo sapiens, Escherichia coli and Panthera leo are written this way in every scientific publication.
items.specStatementText: The two-part scientific name
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the genetic variation between two humans larger or smaller than the variation between a human and a chimpanzee?
items.correct: Much smaller. Any two humans differ at roughly one base in a thousand, whereas the human and chimpanzee genomes differ at a far greater proportion of positions; variation between species is much larger than variation within a species.
items.misconception: Because individual humans differ so obviously in appearance, the genetic differences among humans are about as large as, or larger than, the differences between humans and closely related species.
items.why: Visible variation within a species is what students notice every day, while a chimpanzee and a human are both simply 'apes' at a distance. Popular figures such as 'humans and chimpanzees are 98% similar' sound like a small difference. Genomes vary in base sequence, and the variation between species is much larger than the variation within a species. Two unrelated humans differ at about 0.1% of positions; humans and chimpanzees differ at over 1% of aligned positions and by larger insertions, deletions and rearrangements as well, an overall difference at least ten times greater.
items.specStatementText: Genomes differ in size and sequence, far more between species than within
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can organisms that reproduce only asexually be placed in species?
items.correct: Yes, but not by the biological species concept, which asks whether organisms can breed to produce fertile offspring. Their species are defined on morphological, ecological or DNA sequence similarity instead.
items.misconception: Because asexual organisms never breed, the definition of a species cannot be applied to them, so every clone is its own species or they have no species at all.
items.why: Students apply the biological species concept as if it were the only definition, and follow the logic that an organism that does not breed cannot satisfy it. The biological species concept does not work well for groups of organisms that do not breed sexually. Competing species definitions exist, and for asexual organisms biologists use shared traits and DNA sequence similarity to define species, as Linnaeus originally did on morphology alone.
items.specStatementText: Why the biological species concept fails for asexual organisms and bacteria
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a shared chromosome number show that two organisms belong to the same species?
items.correct: No. The same chromosome number is expected within a species, but different species can have the same number (many mammals have 2n = 48), so it is a necessary rather than a sufficient condition.
items.misconception: Two organisms with the same number of chromosomes are the same species, and two with different numbers cannot be.
items.why: Chromosome number is one of the few numerical traits students meet, and a matching number feels like a definitive fingerprint. Chromosome number is a trait shared within a species, and differing numbers make fertile hybrids unlikely, but many unrelated species happen to share a number. Chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans all have 48 chromosomes and are separate species.
items.specStatementText: Chromosome number is shared within a species
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many choices should each step of a dichotomous key offer?
items.correct: Exactly two contrasting, mutually exclusive alternatives; 'dichotomous' means dividing into two.
items.misconception: Each step of a key can offer as many alternatives as there are types of organism at that point, which makes the key shorter.
items.why: Students want to reach the answer quickly and treat the key as a list of descriptions to match, not as a sequence of binary decisions. The meaning of 'dichotomous' is not obvious from the word. A dichotomous key is a series of paired statements, each pair describing contrasting alternatives of one trait, and each alternative leading to an identification or to another pair. Two alternatives at every step keep each decision unambiguous.
items.specStatementText: Building a dichotomous key for local species
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does DNA barcoding involve sequencing an organism's whole genome?
items.correct: No. A barcode is a short, standardized region of DNA (such as part of the COI gene in animals) that varies between species but little within them, compared against a reference database.
items.misconception: To identify a species from its DNA the whole genome must be sequenced and compared with the whole genome of known species.
items.why: Whole genome sequencing is the DNA technique students hear most about, and 'identifying by DNA' is assumed to mean reading all of it. Barcoding uses a short region chosen because its sequence differs between species and is nearly constant within a species. Sequencing only this region from many organisms or from environmental DNA is fast and cheap, which is what allows the biodiversity of a habitat to be investigated rapidly.
items.specStatementText: Reading a habitat's species from environmental DNA
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What makes a hypothesis testable?
items.correct: That it makes predictions which can be checked against observations or experiments and could turn out to be wrong; whether scientists currently accept it is irrelevant.
items.misconception: 'Testable' means 'proven': a hypothesis becomes testable, or scientific, once enough scientists agree that it is true.
items.why: Students hear 'tested' and 'proven' used interchangeably in everyday speech, and science is presented as a body of accepted facts, so acceptance by experts is taken as the mark of a scientific claim. Testability is a property of the claim, not of its popularity. The chromosome 2 fusion hypothesis was testable before any evidence was gathered, because it predicted internal telomere sequences and a second centromere region that might not have been there. A non-testable statement, however widely believed, makes no prediction that could fail.

items.q: What does a dark band on a stained chromosome in a karyogram represent?
items.correct: A region of the chromosome that takes up the stain strongly, reflecting its DNA composition and packing. A band spans a very large stretch of DNA that may contain many genes or almost none, so a band is not a gene, and the same coarse banding at one part of two chromosomes does not mean they carry the same genes.
items.misconception: Each band is a gene, so two chromosomes with the same pattern of bands carry the same genes and must be a homologous pair.
items.why: Chromosome diagrams in textbooks label gene loci alongside bands, and 'gene mapping' is discussed in the same lessons as banding, so students merge the two ideas. The bands are the only visible subdivision of a chromosome and are taken to be its units, the genes. Bands are produced by stains such as Giemsa binding unevenly along the chromosome; they are a feature of large regions of DNA, not of single genes, and they are the same in every normal cell of a species. Banding pattern is one of three features used to classify chromosomes, together with length and centromere position; a pair is only homologous when all three match.
